name: Rancher
license: Apache 2.0 (Rancher Prime is a paid subscription)
summary: SUSE’s open-source control plane for fleets of Kubernetes clusters: one place to create, import, secure and upgrade them.
intro: Rancher is itself a Kubernetes application. You install it with Helm onto a small Kubernetes cluster (the “local” cluster), and it then manages any number of “downstream” clusters. It can create them (RKE2 or K3s on VMs or bare metal it provisions through cloud drivers, or hosted EKS, AKS and GKE clusters through their APIs) or import any existing conformant cluster. In each downstream cluster a `cattle-cluster-agent` opens a tunnel back to the Rancher server, so the connection starts from inside each managed cluster.

On top of that link Rancher adds what plain Kubernetes leaves to you across many clusters: one login backed by Active Directory, GitHub, Okta or other identity providers, an authentication proxy that impersonates each user on the target cluster, RBAC templates and “projects” (groups of namespaces) applied everywhere, a web UI, a Helm app catalog, Fleet for GitOps deployments to many clusters at once, and Prometheus-based monitoring. For RKE2 and K3s clusters it also handles Kubernetes upgrades and etcd snapshots through an agent on every node.
strengths: Manages almost any cluster: ones it creates, hosted EKS, AKS and GKE, and imported clusters from any conformant distribution
Central identity and RBAC: users log in once and get consistent permissions on every cluster
Agents open the connection from inside each cluster, which suits clusters at the edge, behind NAT or in other clouds
The full platform is open source under Apache 2.0 and free to run; Prime adds support, not a different codebase
limits: Rancher is one more critical system to run, back up and upgrade; for production it should sit on its own HA Kubernetes cluster
Deepest integration is with SUSE’s own RKE2 and K3s; imported and hosted clusters get fewer lifecycle features
Recent patch releases for older minor lines (such as v2.14.5 in August 2026) shipped as Prime builds, so community users need to track the newest minor version
Longer support windows, signed images with SBOMs from a trusted registry and SUSE support require a Rancher Prime subscription

story: Rancher Labs was founded in Cupertino in 2014 by Sheng Liang, Shannon Williams, Darren Shepherd and Will Chan. Docker had just made containers easy to build and run on one machine, but running them across many machines was still unsolved, and there was no clear winner among orchestrators. Rancher 1.0, released in March 2016, hedged: it shipped its own orchestrator, Cattle, and could also set up Kubernetes or Docker Swarm environments.

As Kubernetes pulled ahead of the other orchestrators, Rancher 2.0 (May 2018) was redesigned around it. Instead of being one more orchestrator, Rancher became a manager of many Kubernetes clusters, including EKS, AKS and GKE ones, with its own installer, RKE. The company then built K3s (2019) for the edge and RKE2 (2020) for regulated datacenters. SUSE agreed to buy Rancher Labs in July 2020 and closed the deal on December 1, 2020.

Under SUSE, Rancher stayed Apache-licensed, and SUSE sells it as Rancher Prime: the same code with support, longer lifecycles and a trusted image registry. RKE1, the Docker-based installer from 2.0, reached end of life in July 2025.

choices.choice: Run the management server on Kubernetes itself
choices.why: From 2.0, the Rancher server is built on an embedded Kubernetes API server and etcd, and stores its own objects as Kubernetes resources. Its controllers then work like any other Kubernetes controller, reconciling desired and actual state of downstream clusters.

Each downstream cluster’s agent opens a tunnel to the Rancher server rather than Rancher reaching in, so a cluster only needs to be able to reach Rancher, which suits clusters behind firewalls or NAT and at the edge.

Rather than insist on its own distribution, Rancher 2.0 shipped integrations for GKE, EKS and AKS and could import any cluster, betting that companies would end up with several kinds of Kubernetes and need one place to govern them.

timeline.text: Rancher Labs founded; the rancher/rancher repository is created in November
Rancher 1.0 GA in March, with Cattle, Kubernetes and Swarm environments
Rancher 2.0 in May, redesigned to manage many Kubernetes clusters
K3s released for edge and small clusters
SUSE agrees to buy Rancher Labs in July and completes the deal on December 1
